extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, dramatists, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, song) according to Aristotle's Poetics. Focuses on the elements, structure, and effects a tragedy must have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its nature: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of these parts (Song and Diction) constitute the medium of imitation; one (the manner) is Diction; three are objects of imitation. All of these elements are found in every play, though emphasis varies. Treat each as a distinct component when constructing or judging a tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot (the arrangement of the incidents) is the first principle and the most important element of Tragedy; the Plot is the imitation of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play with a well-constructed plot produces the essential tragic effect even if deficient in diction or character. Novices often attain diction and portraiture before they can construct plot; thus plot-making is the defining task of the poet/maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; it reveals moral purpose, showing what a man chooses or avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is subsidiary to action: dramatic action is not with a view to the representation of character but character comes in to serve actions. Speeches that do not display choice or avoidance are not expressive of character. Tragedy can exist without character, but cannot exist without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (intellectual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; it is where something is proved or a general truth enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought corresponds to the function of rhetoric/oratory in speech; it should make statements that demonstrate reasoning, maxim, or decisive judgement relevant to the action. Use Thought to show deliberation and to advance the plot logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction is the medium of imitation (with Song). It should express meaning clearly and appropriately to the character and situation; good diction alone cannot substitute for a well-constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (musical element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the embellishments, Song holds the chief place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song is an important embellishment of tragic performance and contributes to effect, but it is subordinate to Plot. Treat Song as a chief ornament that enhances but does not substitute for structural elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has an emotional attraction of its own but is the least artistic of the parts and is least connected with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects depend more on the art of the stage machinist than on the poet. While spectacle increases immediate sensory impact, it should not be relied on as the primary source of tragic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness and completeness of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be an imitation of an action that is complete and whole: a whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A beginning is something which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end naturally follows something else; a middle follows and is followed. A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to these causal principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and order
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful tragic whole must be of a certain magnitude and have an orderly arrangement of parts; beauty depends on magnitude and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too small a dramatic piece is confused (seen in an almost imperceptible moment); too large a piece loses unity because the eye/memory cannot take it all in. The proper magnitude is roughly that which can be embraced by memory and permits a clear sequence allowing a change of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in imitation of one action (a single, whole action) whose parts are so organized that removing any part disjoints the whole; unity is not achieved by merely focusing on one hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the many incidents in one man's life with a single unified action. Compose the plot to centre around a single action with organic structural union among parts (every part must make a visible difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/necessity over mere sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should relate what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity, not merely what has happened; poetry aims at the universal (what a person of a certain type would do), history at the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should show causally or probabilistically connected incidents. Avoid episodic ‘stringing together’ of incidents without probable or necessary sequence — that is an anti-pattern of bad plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots may be Simple (change of fortune without Reversal or Recognition) or Complex (change accompanied by Reversal of Intention, Recognition, or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots, with Reversal and/or Recognition arising from the plot's internal structure, are generally superior because they produce stronger tragic effects (pity and fear). Choose type consciously according to desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of Intention (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of Intention is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, consistent with probability or necessity (e.g., a messenger meant to relieve creates the opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should arise from the internal structure of the plot so that outcomes are the necessary or probable results of prior events. Properly executed reversals intensify the tragic effect by turning expectation into the opposite outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; best when coincident with Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition may be of persons or facts and can arise from trivial signs. When recognition coincides with reversal it most powerfully produces pity and fear; ensure recognitions are motivated by the plot, not contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action (e.g., death on the stage, lamentations, wounds) included as part of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic incidents are among the parts that produce emotional effects; they must be integrated causally into the plot rather than included for mere shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts and their definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into Prologue, Episode, Exodos, and Choric song (the latter divided into Parodos and Stasimon); the Commos and actor-songs are peculiar to some plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prologos: part preceding Parodos. Episode: parts between complete choric songs. Exodos: final part with no choric song after it. Parodos: Chorus's first utterance. Stasimon: choric ode without certain metres. Use these divisions to structure action and rhythm of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic plotting and overextension
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad poets compose episodic plots where episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; good poets avoid stretching plots merely to please actors or competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stretch the plot beyond its natural capacity for the sake of showpieces; overextension breaks natural continuity and weakens unity. Ensure each episode has causal or probable connection to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to produce pity, fear, and tragic wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: The most powerful elements of emotional interest in Tragedy (Peripeteia and Recognition) produce pity and fear; the tragic 'wonder' is strongest when events have the air of design rather than accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that reversals and recognitions are surprising yet necessary/probable — coincidences should feel designed. The poet should aim for these effects rather than mere spectacle or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker of plots, not merely versifier
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker should be the maker of plots rather than of verses; a poet imitates actions and thus must shape incidents into a coherent action even when using historical subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the engineering of action and causal sequence; good versification and character portraiture are insufficient without plot construction. Historical materials can be poetically shaped so long as they conform to probable/universal action.
